title: Hot Flashpoints 1950-62
welcome_lead: Korea, Hungary, Berlin and Cuba: the crises that defined the early Cold War.
meta_desc: A-Level adventure on the Korean War 1950-53, Hungary 1956, Berlin Wall 1961 and the Cuban Missile Crisis 1962.
final_note: You can compare the management of nuclear-age crises.

walkthroughs.body_html: Stalin approved Kim Il-sung's invasion on 25 June 1950. The UN Security Council (Soviet boycott) authorised intervention. MacArthur's Inchon landing (September 1950) reversed the tide, but Chinese intervention (October-November 1950) forced retreat. The front stabilised near the 38th parallel; the armistice signed at Panmunjom on 27 July 1953 entrenched division. About 3 million Koreans and 36,000 Americans died.

Khrushchev's Secret Speech (February 1956) raised hopes in Eastern Europe. Polish unrest in June was contained; Hungary went further. Imre Nagy declared neutrality and withdrew from the Warsaw Pact; Soviet tanks invaded on 4 November 1956. In Berlin, East-West economic gulf produced a mass exodus; on 13 August 1961 the GDR sealed the border.

After the Bay of Pigs fiasco (April 1961) and Vienna Summit, Khrushchev placed missiles in Cuba. U-2 photographs (14 October 1962) revealed them. Kennedy imposed a naval 'quarantine' on 22 October. Direct correspondence and the secret Jupiter deal led to Soviet withdrawal on 28 October 1962. The Moscow-Washington hotline followed (1963), as did the Limited Test Ban Treaty.

mcqs.q: How was the Cuban Missile Crisis resolved?
options: The Truman Doctrine ordered the dropping of the atomic bomb on Japan.
The crisis ended when Castro persuaded Khrushchev to withdraw.
Kennedy stared Khrushchev down and the Soviets backed off unconditionally.
A secret deal: the USSR withdrew missiles from Cuba; the US publicly pledged not to invade Cuba and secretly agreed to remove Jupiter missiles from Turkey.

The Truman Doctrine ordered the dropping of the atomic bomb on Japan.
Supporting free peoples resisting communist takeover — initially Greece and Turkey — formalising the policy of containment articulated by George Kennan.
It began when the USSR shot down a US spy plane.
